excerpt: Use file transcription when you have a completed recording or a bounded audio request. Upload the audio and receive a final transcript
Upload the audio and receive a final transcript, or stream text while the model processes the file.
Files can be up to 25 MB. Supported input formats are `mp3`, `mp4`, `mpeg`, `mpga`, `m4a`, `wav`, and `webm`.
The model returns the transcript and the detected languages as JSON
Use `prompt`, `keywords`, and `languages` with `gpt-transcribe` to improve transcription of domain terms and multilingual audio
openai audio:transcriptions create --model gpt-transcribe --file /path/to/file/audio.mp3
You can download and install (or update to) the latest release of Whisper with the following command: pip install -U openai-whisper
The following command will transcribe speech in audio files, using the `turbo` model: whisper audio.flac audio.mp3 audio.wav --model turbo
There are six model sizes, four with English-only versions, offering speed and accuracy tradeoffs.
to transcribe an audio file containing non-English speech, you can specify the language: whisper japanese.wav --language Japanese
To **translate** speech into English, use: whisper japanese.wav --model medium --language Japanese --task translate
Transcription can also be performed within Python: model = whisper.load_model("turbo") result = model.transcribe("audio.mp3")
`whisper.detect_language()` and `whisper.decode()` which provide lower-level access to the model.
a multitasking model that can perform multilingual speech recognition, speech translation, and language identification.
capable of transcribing speech audio into the text in the language it is spoken (ASR) as well as translated into English (speech translation).

A user tried Whisper when it first came out on a 12th-gen i7 laptop in CPU mode. They found the larger, more accurate models took enormous amounts of time without a CUDA-capable GPU, and they are considering buying a desktop with a discrete GPU.

Skeptic: there are tons of open-source STT models, so what makes Whisper so valuable? On iOS, the built-in STT is real-time with punctuation. Whisper didn't strike them as particularly better than other open-source or built-in models.
A user who tried the medium Whisper model in the C/C++ CPU port felt it made more mistakes than the GPU (PyTorch) version.
A user praised whisper.cpp for doing state-of-the-art voice recognition without the PyTorch baggage. They said it runs faster than real time even on a low-spec device.

A user with no C/C++ knowledge edited the whisper.cpp code for their use case and connected it to a Python front end. They call it a game changer for accessibility: 'it can caption almost anything in live!'
A user cloned the whisper.cpp repo on an Apple Silicon Mac and ran the streaming sample, which 'worked flawlessly.'
A user wants to restrict Whisper to a limited vocabulary and get per-word confidence levels for their app. They asked whether that is possible, which suggests it isn't readily supported.
A user says CPU inference for Whisper is not cost-effective for their use case and asked about GPU inference improvements.
A user reported facing problems combining pyannote with Whisper for diarization plus transcription. Whisper transcripts lack speaker labels, so they were experimenting with NeMo plus Whisper instead.
A user tried a Whisper-plus-diarization pipeline on a technical talk, and it got the number of speakers wrong.
A user ran Buzz (real-time mic transcription with Whisper) on Ubuntu 20.x. It seemed to work fine, except the stop button did nothing, so they couldn't stop it to copy the text.
